newsitem.title: TURKEY: British envoy says Cyprus talks to be lengthy.
newsitem.headline: British envoy says Cyprus talks to be lengthy.

text.p: Britain's special envoy to Cyprus predicted on Friday that talks next month between the leaders of the divided island's Greek and Turkish communities were unlikely to produce any quick breakthrough.

"I think there will not be a very rapid conclusion to these negotiations," envoy Sir David Hannay told Reuters in Turkey. "The breaking down of barriers will inevitably be a slow and lengthy process," he said.
Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash are to meet in New York state on July 9 for U.N.-brokered talks.
Western diplomats say the meeting, the first between the pair for nearly three years, may be followed by two further encounters in August and September.
"What I do think is a possible objective...would be what I would call an early harvest. That is to say, some significant signs of progress after the first two or three sessions," Hannay said.
Cyprus has been divided since Turkey invaded in 1974 in response to a Greek Cypriot coup backed by Athens. Previous international attempts to reunify the Mediterranean island have failed.

The talks come against a backdrop of increased concern at the risks of militarisation in Cyprus and membership talks next year between the the European Union and the Greek Cypriot administration, recognised abroad as the island's legitimate government.
The breakaway self-declared Turkish Cypriot state, headed by Denktash, is only recognised by Ankara.
President Bill Clinton last week appointed Richard Holbrooke as the U.S. special emissary for Cyprus. Holbrooke won fame as the tough negotiator of the 1995 Bosnia peace accord at Dayton, Ohio.
Hannay said a similar, go-for-broke agreement was not expected on the Cyprus issue. "Cyprus is quite different and I notice that Dick Holbrooke has been taking a quite different line about it."
A government comprising both Greek and Turkish Cypriots formed after independence from Britain in 1960 broke down in 1963.
